lessons.title: Traveling and the gather step
lessons.objective: Explain the gather step and why travel calls confuse everyone.

payload.prompt: A handler catches a pass and takes two steps before shooting. Traveling?

options.text: Yes, always a travel
No, the gather step doesn't count against the two-step limit
Only if both feet land at the same time

explanation.correct: Right. The gather step—securing the ball—doesn't count. After gathering, two more steps are legal. That's three footfalls total.
explanation.incorrect: The gather is free. After securing the ball, two steps are allowed. Three steps total from the gather is legal.
explanation.sayThisLine: Gather, step one, step two. That's legal.

payload.prompt: A handler does a euro step: left, then right, evading the defender. Legal?

options.text: No, you can only step in one direction
Yes, as long as the steps come after the gather
Only if the defender is moving

explanation.correct: Correct. The euro step is legal in the NBA and college. First step one way, second step the other way, both after the gather.
explanation.incorrect: The euro step is legal. The ball handler takes one step to one side then one to the other, both counted as the two allowed steps after the gather.
explanation.sayThisLine: Euro step is two steps in different directions. It's legal.

payload.prompt: A player catches the ball and pivots on their right foot, rotating 360 degrees. Legal?

options.text: Yes, a pivot foot can rotate any amount
No, you can only pivot 180 degrees
Only in the post

explanation.correct: Yes. A player with the ball can pivot on a planted foot as many times as they want. The foot must stay on the floor.
explanation.incorrect: Once you have the ball, plant one foot as your pivot foot and rotate it as many times as you wish. The foot must stay in contact with the floor.
explanation.sayThisLine: Plant a pivot foot and you can spin all day.

payload.prompt: Ball handler gathers and takes four steps before shooting. Traveling?

scene.alt: A ball handler secures the ball and takes four visible steps toward the basket.

explanation.correct: Yes, traveling. Gather step plus two is the limit. Four steps means one too many.
explanation.incorrect: After the gather, only two steps are allowed. Four total steps is traveling.
explanation.sayThisLine: Gather, one, two—that's all. Four steps is a travel.

statement.speaker: Alex
statement.text: He traveled for sure, too many steps.

payload.question: What does he mean?

options.text: The player took too many steps without dribbling
The player moved out of bounds
The player moved more than two steps after catching the ball
The player took a flight somewhere

payload.translation: After catching the ball, the player took more than two steps without dribbling it, which is a violation.

followUps.why: Tests if they know gather doesn't count toward the limit.

followUps.line: Do all refs call it the same way?

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Travel calls are famously inconsistent; saying 'that looked like a travel' is safe.

lessons.title: Dribbling violations
lessons.objective: Tell a double dribble from a carry from a clean dribble.

payload.prompt: A dribbler uses both hands to bounce the ball at the same time. Violation?

scene.alt: A dribbler using both hands to bounce the ball at the same time.

explanation.correct: Yes, double dribble. Using both hands on the same dribble is a violation.
explanation.incorrect: Double dribble happens when a player dribbles with both hands at once or touches the ball with both hands during a dribble.
explanation.sayThisLine: Double-dribbled, both hands on the ball.

payload.prompt: A dribbler palms the ball (lets it rest in their hand) while moving. Violation?

scene.alt: A ball handler holding the ball in their palm while not bouncing it.

explanation.correct: Yes. Carrying (palming) is a dribble violation. The ball must bounce, not rest in the palm.
explanation.incorrect: When a dribbler carries or palms the ball, they lose control. It is a turnover.
explanation.sayThisLine: He carried it, that's a turnover.

payload.prompt: A handler brings the ball into the front court, then dribbles it back across half court. Violation?

scene.alt: A player advancing the ball into the opponent's half, then dribbling back across half court.

explanation.correct: Yes, backcourt violation. Once a player brings the ball across half court, they cannot bring it back.
explanation.incorrect: Once a player crosses half court into the front court, they cannot dribble it back across half court.
explanation.sayThisLine: Backcourt, he brought it back across half.

payload.prompt: A player dribbles, picks up the ball, holds it, then dribbles again. Violation?

scene.alt: A dribbler stopping the dribble, cradling the ball, then resuming the dribble.

explanation.correct: Yes, double dribble. Once the dribble ends, you cannot dribble again without a pass.
explanation.incorrect: Once the dribble ends (the ball is caught), you can only shoot, pass, or pivot. Dribbling again is a double-dribble violation.
explanation.sayThisLine: Picked it up and dribbled again, that's a double.

payload.prompt: Which signal means double dribble or carry?

image.alt: Referee hand signals showing a rolling hands over each other motion.

options.text: Rolling hands continuously
Single arm rolling motion
Sweeping arm horizontally
Three fingers up

explanation.correct: Right. The ref rolls both hands over each other to signal double dribble or carry.
explanation.incorrect: Refs signal dribble violations with rolling hands—the motion mimics a bouncing ball rolling.

payload.prompt: When the ref sees a player carrying the ball, what happens?

options.text: Award a free throw
Call a turnover; the other team gets the ball
Give a technical foul

explanation.correct: The ball is turned over to the other team. It is not a foul, but a violation.
explanation.incorrect: Dribble violations like carrying result in a turnover. The opposing team gets possession.

payload.prompt: Match the violation to the time limit it involves.

pairs.definition: Offensive player stays in the paint for more than 3 seconds while their team has the ball.
Inbounder takes over 5 seconds to get the ball in play or closely guarded player holds the ball over 5 seconds.
Team fails to get the ball across half court within 8 seconds (ten in college).
Team fails to get a shot off before the shot clock expires: 24 sec NBA/WNBA, 30 in college.

explanation.summary: These clock rules keep the game moving and prevent endless stalling in any area.
explanation.sayThisLine: Three seconds in the lane, eight to cross half, 24 on the shot clock.

payload.prompt: Post player stands in the paint for 4 seconds while their team has the ball. Violation?

scene.alt: A player standing in the painted lane area with the ball on the perimeter.

explanation.correct: Yes, 3-second violation. The limit is three seconds on offense. Four is too long.
explanation.incorrect: An offensive player can spend at most 3 consecutive seconds in the paint. Four seconds is a violation.
explanation.sayThisLine: Three seconds max in the lane on offense.

payload.prompt: A team takes 10 seconds to get the ball across half court in the NBA. Violation?

scene.alt: A team slowly advancing the ball down court past the half-court line.

explanation.correct: Yes, 8-second violation. In the NBA, a team has eight seconds. Ten is too slow.
explanation.incorrect: The NBA and WNBA allow eight seconds to cross half court. College is ten. Ten seconds in the NBA is a turnover.
explanation.sayThisLine: Eight seconds to get up court in the NBA.

payload.prompt: Shot clock shows 2 sec; a player throws the ball up as the clock hits zero. Does it count?

scene.alt: A desperation heave released as the shot clock expires, missing the rim entirely.

explanation.correct: Shot-clock violation. The ball must leave the player's hands before the clock expires and must hit the rim or go in.
explanation.incorrect: For a shot to count, it must leave the shooter's hands before time and hit the rim (or go in). Airball after the buzzer is a violation.
explanation.sayThisLine: Airball after the shot clock. No good.

payload.prompt: Complete the clock rules for the NBA.
payload.template: A team has {{eight}} seconds to get the ball across half court and {{twentyfour}} seconds to shoot it.

explanation.correct: Right. Eight to cross half, 24 to shoot in the NBA. College is ten and 30.
explanation.incorrect: NBA rules: eight seconds to get across half court, 24 seconds for a shot. These times differ in college and the WNBA.

lessons.title: Personal and shooting fouls
lessons.objective: Sort fouls by type and explain the and-one.

payload.prompt: A defender pushes an offensive player away from the ball. What foul is this?

options.text: Shooting foul
Personal foul
Technical foul

explanation.correct: Personal foul. Pushing, holding or elbowing is contact away from a shot attempt.
explanation.incorrect: Contact away from a shot is a personal foul. If it happens while shooting, it's a shooting foul.

payload.prompt: A defender fouls a shooter and the shot goes in. What happens?

options.text: The basket doesn't count
The basket counts and the player shoots one free throw (and-one)
The basket counts and the player shoots two free throws

explanation.correct: Correct. Made shot plus a foul equals an and-one: the basket counts, plus one free throw.
explanation.incorrect: When a shooter is fouled and makes the shot, it's an and-one: the basket counts and they get one bonus free throw.

payload.prompt: A player gets their sixth personal foul in the NBA. What happens?

options.text: They sit out one quarter
They are fouled out and must leave the game
They lose two free throws

explanation.correct: They foul out and are ejected. Six fouls disqualifies a player in the NBA and WNBA. College is five.
explanation.incorrect: In the NBA and WNBA, a sixth personal foul disqualifies the player. They must leave the game.

payload.prompt: Order the events when a player is fouled while shooting and makes the basket.

items.why: The foul happens during the shot attempt.
The shot goes in before or after the foul call.

items.text: Player goes to the free-throw line
items.why: The and-one free throw is awarded.

explanation.correct: Foul called, basket counts, then one free throw is shot. That's an and-one.
explanation.incorrect: When fouled while shooting successfully: foul, basket counts, player shoots one bonus free throw.

payload.prompt: How many personal fouls does a player need in the NBA before fouling out?

explanation.correct: Six fouls in the NBA and WNBA. College is five.
explanation.incorrect: A player fouls out at six personal fouls in the NBA and WNBA. College is five fouls.

statement.speaker: Jordan
statement.text: He's in the bonus, so we get two free throws on the next foul.

payload.question: What does he mean?

options.text: The other team has committed enough fouls that all future fouls result in free throws
A player just made a three-pointer and gets extra points
The team has earned a reward for playing defense
Subsequent fouls will be non-shooting fouls

payload.translation: The other team has committed enough fouls in the quarter (five in the NBA) that your team is now in the team-foul bonus. Every additional foul will send your team to the free-throw line for two shots.

followUps.line: How many fouls until the bonus kicks in?
followUps.why: Tests knowledge of the foul limit.

followUps.line: Do you reset the count each quarter?

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Asking 'how many team fouls did they have?' is always safe.

lessons.title: Free throws, the bonus and techs
lessons.objective: Explain bonus, technical, flagrant and intentional fouls.

payload.prompt: Match the foul type to its definition.

pairs.definition: A non-contact foul for unsporting conduct, arguing with the ref, delay of game, or other violations. Awards one free throw.
Excessive or unnecessary contact that endangers an opponent. Results in two free throws and a possession.
Extreme excessive force or dangerous play, resulting in ejection plus two free throws and possession.
A deliberate foul (not based on judgment) to stop play or prevent an easy basket.

explanation.summary: Fouls outside normal contact (technical), excessively hard contact (flagrant), and deliberate stops (intentional) all have distinct penalties.

payload.prompt: A coach yells at the referee, 'That's a terrible call!' The ref points at the coach. What is called?

options.text: Technical foul on the coach
Unsportsmanlike conduct on the player
Delay of game

explanation.correct: Technical foul. Arguing or complaining to the ref earns a tech.
explanation.incorrect: A coach or player arguing with the referee or being disrespectful receives a technical foul.

payload.prompt: The opposing team has committed five fouls in the quarter in the NBA. What happens on the next foul?

options.text: Regular play continues, no free throws
Your team shoots two free throws
Your team shoots one free throw and keeps the ball

explanation.correct: Your team is in the bonus and shoots two free throws on every subsequent foul (even non-shooting fouls).
explanation.incorrect: Once a team reaches five fouls in a quarter (NBA), the other team is in the bonus and shoots two free throws for all future fouls.

payload.prompt: A defender elbows an offensive player hard while driving. This is ruled flagrant-2. What is the consequence?

options.text: Two free throws and the fouled player keeps the ball
Two free throws, the fouled team gets possession, and the defender is ejected
One technical free throw and a technical is charged

explanation.correct: Flagrant-2 results in ejection (throw-out), two free throws, and possession. Excessive force is not tolerated.
explanation.incorrect: A flagrant-2 foul is extreme. The player is ejected, the opponent shoots two free throws, and gets the ball back.

payload.prompt: Complete the NBA bonus foul rule.
payload.template: When a team commits {{count}} fouls in a quarter, the opposing team shoots {{shots}} free throws on all subsequent fouls.

explanation.correct: Right. Five fouls = bonus. Two free throws on every foul thereafter. College: seven for one-and-one, ten for two.
explanation.incorrect: NBA: five fouls in a quarter triggers the bonus. All subsequent fouls = two free throws.

lessons.title: Charge or block?
lessons.objective: Judge charge vs block using position, feet and the restricted-area arc.

payload.prompt: Defender is standing still with feet planted and arms up. An offensive player drives into them. Charge or block?

scene.alt: A stationary defender with feet planted, arms raised. An offensive player collides into the defender's chest.

explanation.correct: Charge. The defender was set first (feet planted, legal position) before the offensive player initiated contact.
explanation.incorrect: If the defender establishes legal guarding position (feet on floor, hands up or down) before the offensive player commits to driving into them, it's a charge.

payload.prompt: A help defender is in the restricted arc under the basket. An offensive player drives into them. Can it be a charge?

scene.alt: A defender in the restricted arc touching the offensive player driving to the basket.

explanation.correct: Block. A defender in the restricted area cannot draw a charge; it's automatically a blocking foul (unless the defender is the primary defender).
explanation.incorrect: Secondary defenders in the restricted arc cannot draw a charge. Contact in that area is a blocking foul on the defender.

payload.prompt: A defender has hands straight up (vertical) and does not move. An offensive player runs into the defender's hands. Foul?

scene.alt: A defender with arms raised straight up, standing still. An offensive player collides into the vertical hands.

explanation.correct: No foul. Verticality allows a defender to move arms straight up. If the ball handler runs into vertical hands, the ball handler committed the foul.
explanation.incorrect: A defender can move arms vertically without fouling. If the ball handler runs into vertical hands, the ball handler committed the foul, not the defender.

payload.prompt: Tap the restricted area (the 4-foot arc where charges cannot be drawn).

diagram.alt: A basketball court showing the restricted area arc under both baskets.

explanation.correct: Right. The restricted area is the 4-foot arc. Help defenders here cannot draw charges.
explanation.incorrect: The restricted area is the arc under the basket. Secondary defenders in this area commit a blocking foul if contact occurs.

statement.speaker: Casey
statement.text: That was a charge, he wasn't even in position.

payload.question: What is Casey saying?

options.text: The defender was not set before the offensive player made contact
The defender had an illegal position when contact happened
The call was a block but should have been a charge
The defender moved into the path after the play started

payload.translation: Casey believes the defensive player was not set or established legal guarding position in time, so contact is a blocking foul on the defender, not a charge on the ball handler. The defender should not have been called for a charge.

followUps.line: Were they in the restricted area?
followUps.why: Tests if location changes the call.

followUps.line: Did the defender have time to get set?

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Charge-block is one of the most debated calls in basketball. Saying 'I thought it was a charge' is always okay.

lessons.title: Goaltending and basket interference
lessons.objective: Know when a ball on the way down or up can no longer be touched.

payload.prompt: A shot is heading downward toward the rim when a defender taps it away. Goaltending?

scene.alt: A shot falling toward the basket is touched by a defender before it hits the rim.

explanation.correct: Yes, goaltending. Once a shot is on its way down toward the basket or on the rim, it cannot be touched. The basket counts automatically.
explanation.incorrect: Goaltending occurs when a player touches a shot that is heading down toward the basket or already on the rim.

payload.prompt: A ball bouncing up off the rim toward the basket is swatted by a defender. Goaltending?

scene.alt: A ball bouncing up from the rim is struck by a defender's hand.

explanation.correct: Yes, goaltending. A ball on the rim bouncing upward is still part of a live shot. Touching it is goaltending.
explanation.incorrect: Goaltending includes any touch of a ball that is above the rim or on the rim, whether falling or rising.

payload.prompt: A shot bounces off the rim, clears the rim area completely, and is on the way down again. Can a defender touch it now?

scene.alt: A rebound falling back down toward the basket after bouncing away from the rim.

explanation.correct: Legal. Once the ball clears the rim and basket area, it's a live rebound. Anyone can grab it.
explanation.incorrect: Goaltending only applies to a live shot attempt. Once a rebound clears the basket area, it is a free ball.

payload.prompt: Tap the area where touching the rim or backboard can result in basket interference.

diagram.alt: A close-up of the basketball rim, backboard and net, showing the area where interference can occur.

explanation.correct: Right. Basket interference involves the rim, backboard, or net while a shot is in the air.
explanation.incorrect: Basket interference is illegally touching the rim, backboard, or net during a live shot attempt.

payload.prompt: A player reaches through the net and touches the ball as it falls into the basket. What happens?

options.text: The basket does not count
The basket counts anyway (basket interference does not negate a made basket)
Two free throws are awarded instead

explanation.correct: The basket counts. Basket interference is a violation, but a made basket still counts. It's a technical situation.
explanation.incorrect: Unlike goaltending, basket interference does not negate a made basket. The basket counts and it is a violation on the defender.

lessons.title: Replay, challenges and the L2M
lessons.objective: Explain replay review, coach challenges and the last-two-minute report.

payload.prompt: Which referee hand signal indicates a foul?

image.alt: Four different referee hand signals: waving arms, pointing, arms in a T, and hands on chest.

options.text: Pointing directly at the player
Waving both arms horizontally
Making a T with both arms
Hands placed on chest

explanation.correct: Right. Refs point to indicate a foul and which team gets the ball.
explanation.incorrect: A referee signals a foul by pointing at the player and indicating which team gets the ball.

payload.prompt: What hand signal do referees use to call a timeout?

image.alt: Four referee hand signals: pointing up, making a T with arms, open hand wave, and one arm extended.

options.text: Both arms up in a T shape
One finger pointing up
Open hand wave across chest
One arm extended to the side

explanation.correct: Right. The T signal (hands up and out) means timeout.
explanation.incorrect: Refs signal a timeout by making a T with their arms—one arm vertical, one horizontal.

payload.prompt: How do referees signal a jump ball?

image.alt: Four referee hand signals: pointing up, waving arms in a circle, both hands clasped, and arms extended wide.

options.text: Both hands moving upward with fingers spread
One arm pointing straight up
Arms moving in a circle
Both hands clasped together

explanation.correct: Right. Both hands up with fingers spread indicates a jump ball.
explanation.incorrect: Refs signal a jump ball by moving both hands up with fingers spread open.

payload.prompt: A coach successfully challenges a foul call in the NBA. Can they challenge again later?

options.text: No, one challenge per game
Yes, they get a second challenge
Only if the second challenge is in the final two minutes

explanation.correct: Yes. In the NBA, a coach gets a second challenge if the first is successful. A third challenge is not allowed.
explanation.incorrect: NBA rules as of 2025-26: a coach can challenge once, and if successful, earns a second challenge.

payload.prompt: What is the NBA's Last-Two-Minute (L2M) report?

options.text: A live feed of player statistics in the final minutes
An official document released after games reviewing all calls in the final two minutes
A coach's challenge review system

explanation.correct: The L2M report reviews all fouls and judgment calls in the final two minutes for transparency and accountability.
explanation.incorrect: The NBA releases an L2M report after each game showing all fouls, timing, and whether calls were correct or missed.
